analysis.one_liner: Pays states federal mineral royalties to replace revenue lost when federal oil and gas leasing is paused.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Liz Cheney with one cosponsor, was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The PILLR Act would require the Interior Department to pay states from federal mineral royalties whenever federal oil and gas leasing on their land is paused or stopped by the President or other officials. Payments would cover lost lease bonuses, royalties, and state tax revenues, calculated from a ten-year average of what the state used to receive, adjusted for inflation [S2][S3]. The money would come with strings only in the sense that it is subject to annual congressional appropriation [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: States with federal oil and gas production, whose budgets would be made whole when leasing pauses cut off lease bonuses, royalties, and severance and property tax revenue tied to drilling. The payments would also blunt the financial pressure that leasing moratoriums place on those states to keep drilling, and shield revenues that flow from oil and gas activity within their borders [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires Interior to compensate states for lost lease rentals, bonuses, royalties, and related tax revenues in any year a presidential or agency action halts or reduces federal oil and gas leasing in that state [S3].

Calculates payments from a 10-year average of disbursements to each state, including a share of royalties tied to new-well production, plus the state's average severance, ad valorem, and production tax rates on oil and gas, adjusted annually for inflation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury and, ultimately, other federal mineral royalty recipients: payments come out of federal mineral royalties, so money routed to compensation states is money not available elsewhere, and the standing federal revenue from halted leasing is not replaced [S3].

drawbacks.text: Payments are only authorized subject to appropriation, so states could be promised compensation that Congress never funds [S3].

The formula guarantees states their 10-year average drilling revenue even when leasing is deliberately paused, which would neutralize a main financial lever the federal government has to manage oil and gas development on public land [S3].
Because payments are drawn from the federal mineral royalty pool, compensating some states would come at the expense of the broader pool of federal revenue and other royalty recipients [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, formula-based payments to oil- and gas-dependent state budgets, but only when leasing is paused, and only if Congress funds them. Its main practical effect is to make leasing moratoriums more expensive for the federal government and less painful for producer states, which reduces the policy's reach. It was never advanced, so no cost was incurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and it sat there without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Liz Cheney introduced the bill on November 30, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S5].
On December 16, 2021, it was referred to the subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where no further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
One Republican cosponsored the bill; no other members joined [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal oil and gas leasing policy was left unchanged; no federal mineral royalties were redirected to compensate producer states for paused leasing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal leasing authority; royalty pool untouched

for.name: Rep. Liz Cheney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Natural Resources Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support was Republican — sponsor Cheney and a single GOP cosponsor — and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal land
industries.note: The bill would not pay companies directly, but it would insulate the state revenues that depend on their drilling, making federal leasing pauses far less effective as a check on production. Producers benefit indirectly because the financial consequence of halting leases would be softened. [S3]

State budgets would be reimbursed from federal royalties for lost lease payments and severance and property taxes whenever leasing is paused. This shifts the cost of federal land management decisions onto the federal royalty pool. [S3]

industries.industry: Federal taxpayers and other mineral royalty recipients
industries.note: Compensation payments would be drawn from the federal mineral royalty pool, reducing what is available for other federal purposes, with no replacement of the paused leasing revenue itself. [S3]
